summary:
Soil Help is a field-level risk tool that tells farmers how much soil their land loses to erosion each year and how likely their slopes are to slide during heavy rain. A farmer outlines a field on a lightweight 3D web map. Our backend automatically gathers ten years of NASA GPM IMERG rainfall and Landsat/HLS vegetation data together with elevation, soil and land-cover maps. It then runs two physical models: RUSLE for soil loss and an infinite-slope landslide model with uncertainty analysis. The result is a map of which parts of the field are at risk, a timeline for any chosen dates, the least costly conservation practice (contour farming, strip cropping or terraces), and plain advice in English.

The project turns scattered, expert-only Earth observation data into answers a farmer can act on. It works on low-end phones and slow rural connections, and uses national survey data in the US and global datasets everywhere else. Erosion steadily strips away the most fertile soil, and rain-triggered landslides destroy fields, roads and homes. Early, local warnings help farmers protect both their land and their livelihoods.
details:
What it does and how it works

Soil Help gives a farmer two answers for one specific field: how much soil it loses to water erosion each year, and how likely its slopes are to slide during heavy rain. The farmer outlines the field on a 3D web map, and our backend works out which data to use from the field's location. Fields in the United States use national surveys at 10 m resolution (USGS 3DEP elevation, USDA SSURGO soils and the Cropland Data Layer). Fields anywhere else use global datasets at 30 m (FABDEM elevation, SoilGrids, ISRIC depth to bedrock and ESA WorldCover). In both cases the backend adds ten years of NASA GPM IMERG half-hourly rainfall and Landsat 8/9 and NASA HLS vegetation data. It then runs two physical models side by side. RUSLE estimates soil loss, with rainfall erosivity computed storm by storm and vegetation cover from monthly NDVI. An infinite-slope stability model with a topographic wetness index estimates landslide risk, run with 100 different sets of soil parameters so that each part of the field gets the rainfall at which failure becomes 10 to 90 percent likely. The farmer receives a map of the risky parts of the field, a timeline for any dates they choose, an alert level (low, watch, warning or danger) and the least costly conservation practice that would keep soil loss tolerable.

Benefits

Soil Help turns scattered Earth observation data that normally needs an expert into a plain answer in Turkish or English, with no technical terms on screen. Instead of stopping at a risk score, it recommends a concrete action, such as contour farming, strip cropping, terraces or permanent cover, and shows which months the soil most needs protection. Results are stored per year and combined on demand, so checking a new date range takes about two seconds. The app is built for low-end phones and slow rural connections, and it switches to a flat 2D lite mode automatically when the device or network is weak.

Intended impact

We want farmers to protect their most fertile soil and prepare before dangerous rain, rather than react after a slope has failed. Agricultural extension services and local governments can also use it to find the fields most at risk and focus support there. Because one codebase serves both US fields with detailed survey data and the rest of the world with global datasets, the tool can reach regions that have no national soil survey at all.

Tools and technologies

The backend is written in Python 3.11 with NumPy and rasterio. It pulls data from the Google Earth Engine API, from USDA Soil Data Access through SQL over HTTPS, and from ISRIC web services, and it is covered by more than 80 automated tests. GitHub Actions runs each field's analysis on demand, and the results are stored in Cloudflare R2. The frontend is built with Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript and MapLibre GL JS v5 for the 3D globe, and it is deployed on Vercel. The map uses Esri World Imagery, AWS Terrarium elevation tiles and Natural Earth place names. No special hardware was needed beyond ordinary laptops, and users need only a phone browser.

How it is creative

Erosion and landslides are usually studied separately and at regional scale, but Soil Help brings both hazards together for a single farm field. Rather than giving a simple yes or no, it gives a landslide threshold that accounts for uncertainty, which is more honest given how little is known about soil strength in most places. It also advises the least effort that solves the problem, not just how severe the problem is. Even the loading screen is part of the design: it is the live globe turning into place, so there is no extra image or progress bar to download on a slow connection.

What our team considered

We designed for farmers on weak phones and rural connections, so we kept the app small, avoided API keys and paid services, and added an automatic lite mode. Turkish is the default language, English is available, and every result is phrased without jargon. Because unit mismatches cause most errors in this kind of work, all units are converted at the point where data enters the system. Large datasets are cached so that repeated runs are fast, and we respected data licences such as FABDEM's non-commercial terms. We were also honest about the limits. IMERG averages rainfall over cells about 10 km wide, and our landslide thresholds are not yet calibrated. Our Hurricane Helene test shows this: the satellite rainfall stayed below our field's alert threshold even though the storm triggered thousands of landslides nearby. Calibrating against the USGS Helene landslide inventory is our next step.
